newsitem.title: USA: US, N.Korea far apart in MIA talks - US official.
newsitem.headline: US, N.Korea far apart in MIA talks - US official.

text.p: U.S. and North Korean officials were "far apart" in talks on how to get "the fullest possible accounting" of U.S. servicemen missing in action from the Korean War, a U.S. defence official said on Friday.

The talks began on Sunday and have continued almost every day since. Alan Liotta, deputy head of the United States delegation from the the Defence Department's POW/Missing Personnel Office, said "talks ... are scheduled to go through today. Both sides are far apart."

Liotta said the first ever meeting between between families of U.S. servicemen missing in the Korean War and officials of North Korea was beneficial -- "it puts a human face on the issue" -- but he said he was "not optimistic" that an agreement would be reached.
At a press conference, relatives of the missing servicemen described their decades-long efforts to obtain information about their lost family members.

Nancy Lovell Dean, whose father was shot down over Korea on Dec. 4, 1950, said that if North Korea wanted normalised diplomatic relations with other countries, it must address the question of what happened to unrepatriated prisoners.

Irene Mandra, sister of Sgt. Philip V. Mandra who was last seen in North Korea on Aug. 7, 1952, said she had asked the head of the North Korean delegation for a list of U.S. prisoners of war who allegedly were sent to Siberia.

The discussions are the fourth round of talks between the Pentagon and North Korea on missing U.S. troops. American and North Korean officials last met in New York a year ago, reaching an agreement that led to the recovery of the remains of a U.S. Army corporal north of Pyongyang.
But a second excavation scheduled for the fall of 1996 fell through after a North Korean submarine loaded with commandos ran aground last September off South Korea.
There are still some 8,100 U.S. troops missing from the Korean War. The Pentagon has said it has no evidence that any are being held captive in North Korea.
The current U.S.-North Korean talks have had three purposes, Larry Greer, spokesman for the defence department's POW/Missing Personnel office said.

First, the United States wants to learn more about live sightings of alleged Americans still living in North Korea. Second, it wants access to North Korean military archives. Third, it wants to establish a schedule for continued joint excavations to recover the remains of Americans buried in North Korea.

Washington has chosen 10 sites it considers the most fruitful, Greer said. These were either the sites of U.S. plane crashes or known burial locations of Americans who died in battle or in North Korean prison camps.

He said it was "a certainty" that there were mass graves in North Korea containing the remains of U.S. servicemen. "We know precisely where many of them are located because of all of our thousands of interviews with returned (prisoners of war). In many cases, there are many, many Americans buried in one spot."
The reports from returned American POWs told of men who died from battle wounds and in prison camps and men who were on forced death marches and executed, Greer said.

He said despite dozens of reports coming out of North Korea over the last several years referring to Caucasians living in North Korea, the United States had not been able to corroborate those sightings as being Americans who were held against their will.
The United States does know of four Americans still alive in North Korea who are U.S. Army deserters, Greer said.

He said the United States has asked the North Koreans to grant it access to these men "in order to learn what we could about the other sightings ... We know that some of the sightings are associated with these deserters."
Washington wants access to North Korea's military archives to learn more about Americans who died in North Korean POW camps, Greer said.
Greer said that although the United States covers the costs associated with excavations, recoveries had to be done jointly to aid identification of the remains.
Talks in New York between the United States and South Korea to urge Pyongyang to begin four-way peace talks with China to negotiate a formal end to the 1950-53 Korean War broke off in April.
